prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: I opened with the CMB acoustic-peak work (B008) first, but I have to be honest that nobody else ranked it and that its credit problem is real: five names for three seats, with Planck and Sunyaev's theory on the wrong side of the line. The optical lattice clock is the candidate that survives scrutiny on every axis I care about. It is a discovery-and-invention at the centre in the sense that nature supplied the magic-wavelength condition and the instrument delivered 1e-18 uncertainties. It has independent reproduction in many laboratories, immediate consequences (the pending redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy, constraints on varying constants and on dark-sector couplings), and a two-name attribution, Katori for the magic-wavelength lattice concept and first strontium realisation, Ye for driving it to record accuracy and many-body clock regimes, that all eight colleagues treat as natural. All eight members ranked it, three of them first, and it is the one case where support does not rest on one member's field.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is overlap and novelty: the 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and the 2012 prize covered control of single ions, and the lattice clock leans on both. A second reservation is that the redefinition of the second has not happened yet, and the two-name list leaves out contributors to strontium lattice spectroscopy and the ion-clock tradition. Broad opening support is also not evidence of scientific merit; it may only mean this is the consensus safe option among several experimentalists.

responses.point: The lattice clock is the cleanest case of measurement precision opening new science, with a fair two-person pairing, though the 2005 and 2012 prizes are acknowledged but not credited.
responses.response: I agree on the attribution and the replication record, and I would move it to the top of my list on that basis. I would qualify the novelty point more firmly than you do: the comb and ion-clock prizes honoured tools and a single-ion regime, whereas the lattice clock is a different concept, many atoms cancelling the trapping Stark shift at a magic wavelength. The citation should therefore name the invention itself and not drift into general precision spectroscopy.

responses.point: The lattice clock sits squarely in precision atomic physics, is confirmed by many laboratories, and a two-laureate split is fair.
responses.response: Your point about independent comparisons across JILA, Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE is the strongest maturity argument we have. Where I would qualify your opening: the Katori and Ye split you call fair is cleaner than the credit disputes you note for other precision-measurement candidates. I also share your worry that Katori's concept versus Ye's technical development is judged from general knowledge, and I would flag that for the final round.

responses.point: The Higgs discovery (B054) is foundational, fully mature and arguably overdue, and he ranks it first, with IceCube (B033) second.
responses.response: I do not dispute the scientific weight of the Higgs discovery, but I resist ranking it first. The statutes' three-person limit forces an arbitrary choice among Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee, and any trio compresses thousands of colleagues, whereas the lattice clock has a defensible attribution on the table. On IceCube I agree with you that the diffuse flux is established and that Halzen and Karle are a credible pair, which is why I keep it as an alternative; I would only note that source identification is still thin, so I see it as slightly less mature than the clock.

responses.point: Topological insulators (B019) top his list because the concept translated into material-specific predictions that experiment confirmed, with a theory-plus-experiment trio of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp.
responses.response: That is a serious case and I rank it as my first alternative. My reservation is the same one you list: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe route, and the prize would be rewarding an experiment whose prediction is not credited, while the 2016 topology prize narrows the novelty. If the committee can word the citation as the Z2 theory plus the first observation without implying completeness of credit, I would support it, but I do not think the attribution problem is smaller than for the clock.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the lattice clock sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether Katori and Ye alone fairly cover the lattice-clock concept, or whether other strontium and lattice-spectroscopy contributors should weigh in.
Whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the second, or recognise the science now.
Whether the missing HgTe prediction credit (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) makes B019 an unworkable second choice.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. My documented connections (David Gross as PhD supervisor, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) do not involve any credited name on this shortlist. My own field is string theory and cosmology, so I am an outsider on the atomic-physics and condensed-matter cases.
